title: Vatan Şarkısı: the song and its occasion
short: Kemal's 'Song of the Fatherland', a marching song of Ottoman patriotism; scholars link it both to his play Vatan yahut Silistre (1873) and to later war.
body: Akün's encyclopedia article mentions the well-known 'Vatan' song of the play Vatan yahut Silistre, first staged at the Gedikpaşa theatre on 1 April 1873. The performance set off demonstrations ('Yaşasın vatan! Yaşasın Kemal!'), and within days İbret was closed and Kemal was exiled to Famagusta, though Akün argues the exile was not directly caused by the play. Gibb printed a verse translation of this song in 1882 (refrain: 'We're Ottomans! our lives we give, our gain is glory bright'), saying it was 'composed on the occasion of the last Russian attack on Turkey', that is, the war of 1877–78, and attributing it to a 'Ref'et Beg'. The sources thus disagree on author and occasion; the attribution to Kemal is the accepted one in Turkish scholarship.

sources.cite: Ömer Faruk Akün, 'Nâmık Kemal', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 32 (2006), pp. 361–378

title: Form: a five-line song stanza with a two-line refrain
short: Each stanza has three monorhymed lines followed by a fixed two-line refrain, so the song is built for collective singing.
body: The four stanzas rhyme aaaBB: three lines on a new rhyme (vatandır / bedendir / kefendir; bayrağımızda / dağımızda / toprağımızda; and so on) and then the same couplet, the nakarat or refrain, ending 'alırız biz'. The şarkı was the Ottoman form written to be set to music, typically in four-line stanzas with a repeated line; here the stanza is enlarged with a two-line chorus, as in a European march. The plural 'biz' (we) throughout makes it a song for a group of volunteers or soldiers, not a lover's private complaint, which is the usual voice of the şarkı.

sources.cite: Mustafa İsmet Uzun, 'Şarkı' (literature), TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 38 (2010), pp. 357–358

title: Metre: hezec-i ahreb
short: The lines scan mef'ûlü mefâîlü mefâîlü feûlün (− − . / . − − . / . − − . / . − −), the metre most used for şarkı.
body: Scanned in aruz, the first line runs Â-mâ-li / mi-zef-kâ-rı / mı-zik-bâ-li / ve-tan-dır, with the final consonants of 'âmâlimiz' and 'efkârımız' carried over (vasl) onto the next vowel. The pattern is mef'ûlü mefâîlü mefâîlü feûlün, the hezec-i ahreb. Topuzoğlu's article on hezec notes that this variety was the metre most often used for the şarkı and for the müstezat. Its galloping opening of two long syllables gives the song its march-like energy; compare the same metre in the rain of snow in Cenab's 'Elhân-ı Şitâ' (ll. 39–50).

title: âmâl, efkâr, ikbâl
greek: Arabic āmāl (pl. of amal 'hope'); afkār (pl. of fikr 'thought'); iqbāl 'good fortune'
short: 'Our hopes, our thoughts are the fatherland's fortune': three Arabic plurals and abstracts made to carry a new political meaning.
body: 'Âmâl' is the Arabic broken plural of emel, hope or ambition; 'efkâr' is the plural of fikr, thought, a word Kemal's generation used for public opinion (as in the newspaper Tasvîr-i Efkâr); 'ikbâl' is prosperity or rising fortune. The line declares that all private hopes and thoughts are absorbed into the good of the vatan. Gibb remarked that Kemal raised 'watan' to the sense of French patrie; the song shows that sense in its most popular form.

title: Bodies as the frontier fortress
greek: Persian sar-ḥadd 'frontier'; Arabic qalʿa 'fortress'; Persian khāk 'dust'
short: The fortress on our frontier is the dust of our bodies: the soldiers themselves are the walls.
body: 'Serhad' (Persian sar-ḥadd) is the frontier, the march where Ottoman ghazi warfare had always been fought; 'kal'a' (Arabic qalʿa) is a fortress; 'hâk-i beden' is the earth or dust of the body. The line fuses two ideas Kemal used repeatedly: that men's bodies are made of the country's soil and that their death on the frontier becomes the frontier's wall. The play Vatan yahut Silistre is set at the defence of the Danube fortress of Silistre in the Crimean War, so the image would have had a concrete referent for its first audience.

title: 'Our ornament is a bloody shroud'
short: The martyr's blood-stained shroud is the Ottomans' only finery.
body: 'Ziynet' (Arabic zīna) is adornment, finery; 'kefen' (Arabic kafan) is the white cloth in which the dead are wrapped. A martyr (şehîd) in Islamic law is buried in the clothes he died in, unwashed, so the 'bloody shroud' is the martyr's mark of honour. Gibb's translation renders it 'a gory shroud our robe of honour grand', bringing out the idea of the robe of honour (hil'at) given by a sultan. The same kanlı kefen appears in Kemal's elegy 'Vâveylâ', where the fatherland itself wears it.

title: Refrain: 'we give our lives, we win a name'
short: The chorus trades life for fame: through martyrdom we gain every desire; we are Ottomans, we give our lives, we take a name.
body: 'In battle, through martyrdom (şehâdet), we obtain all our desire (kâm); we are Ottomans: we give our life, we take a name.' Two value systems meet: the Islamic reward of martyrdom, which opens paradise (st. 4), and the heroic, almost Homeric exchange of life for lasting fame (nâm). The self-name 'Osmanlılarız' is equally telling: it names a political community, not Turks or Muslims as such, in keeping with the Young Ottoman ideal of Ottomanism. Gibb's refrain, 'We're Ottomans! our lives we give, our gain is glory bright', keeps this exchange.

title: The banner: blood and sword
greek: Arabic Dhū l-Faqār (name of Ali's sword)
short: What appears on our banner is blood and a sword, a red field and a blade.
body: The line describes the red Ottoman flag, read as blood, with a sword on it. Gibb's translation reads 'A sabre on a blood-red field', and his note to it explains that the banner of the Janissaries displayed the Zû-'l-Fiqâr, the double-pointed sword of the caliph Ali. Whether Kemal meant a historical banner or the colour of the national flag, the line turns heraldry into a promise of sacrifice. It also shows the song's theatrical character, a tableau the audience can see.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, Ottoman Poems Translated into English Verse in the Original Forms (London: Trübner, 1882), text and notes

title: A lion in every corner
short: In every corner of our land a lion lies: the people are dormant heroes.
body: 'Gûşe' (Persian gōsha) is a corner or nook; 'şîr' (Persian shīr) is the lion. The lion is Kemal's favourite emblem of the people: in the Hürriyet Kasidesi it is chained and then wounded and asleep. Here the verb 'yatar' (lies) is ambiguous: the lion lies in wait, but perhaps lies buried, since 'toprağımızda' (in our soil) suggests the graves of the fallen. Either way the 'fear for life' of the previous line has no place in such a land.

title: fıtrat: inborn nature
short: Do not think our nature has changed: this blood is still the same blood as our ancestors'.
body: 'Fıtrat' (Arabic fiṭra) is the innate nature with which God creates a being. The line answers a fear felt across the late Ottoman world, that the empire's defeats showed a decline of the race. Kemal insists on continuity with the 'heybet' (awe-inspiring majesty) of the ancestors (ecdâd) known to the world. 'Lerze-resân' in the stanza's first line (Persian larza-rasān, 'bringing trembling') makes the Ottoman name itself a cause of fear. Gibb translates the line 'Think not that nature changeth — nay, this blood is yon blood still.'

anchor: Cennet kapısı cân veren ihvâna açılsın
title: The gate of paradise for martyrs
short: Let the cannon roar; let paradise open to the brothers who give their lives; what have we found in this world that we should flee death?
body: The last stanza joins modern artillery (top, cannon) to the Qur'anic promise that those killed in God's way are not dead but living with their Lord (Qur'an 3:169). 'İhvân' (Arabic ikhwān, plural of akh) means brothers, here comrades in arms. The third line is a classical contempt of the world (dünya), a commonplace of Ottoman moralising verse, turned into a reason for courage. The movement from banner to blood to cannon to paradise gives the song a dramatic climax suitable for the stage.

title: Variant text: Gibb's 1882 version
short: Gibb's English version follows a text with a different fourth line and a different stanza order, a sign that the song circulated in variants.
body: Gibb's translation (Ottoman Poems, 1882) has the stanzas in the order 1, 3, 2, 4 of the archive text, and its fourth line in every stanza is a battle cry: '"God is Most Great!" we shout in rush and charge on field of fight', where the archive has 'Gavgâda şehâdetle bütün kâm alırız biz'. Gibb also gives the poet as 'Ref'et Beg' and says the song was composed on the occasion of the last Russian attack on Turkey (the war of 1877–78), on information from H. A. Homes of New York. A song sung in theatres, barracks and schools naturally changes as it travels; the archive text is the one printed by Turkish Wikisource. Students should cite the version they quote.
